title: Live updates from the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand as financial leaders take on AI, debt, and geopolitical upheaval
gist: Atlantic Council live blog from the Oct 2026 IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok: the IMF sees 3.1% growth but 4.7% inflation, bond yields at two-decade highs (US 10y 5.31%), thinning financial safety cushions from AI debt, hedge funds and the Hormuz energy shock, and finance leaders finally treating geopolitics as core to policy.

themes.theme: IMF outlook: growth holds, inflation and debt dominate

insights.claim: The IMF projects global growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, but global headline inflation rising to 4.7 percent in 2026 from 4.1 percent in 2025, with euro area inflation going from 2.1 to 3.1 percent and US from 2.7 to 3.6 percent.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Inflation, not growth, is the main macro story; supports a higher-for-longer rates view.
insights.locator: The new geoeconomics of inflation / Inflation is the biggest concern

insights.claim: Only thirty-two economies now account for 95 percent of global growth, down from fifty-four in the April outlook, and the IMF's baseline is arguably too optimistic.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Narrowing growth base raises fragility if any engine (AI, US, Asia) stalls.
insights.locator: Optimistic growth projections send the wrong message

insights.claim: Growth is bifurcating: economies plugged into AI investment and energy exporters outside the Middle East conflict zone do well, while energy importers outside the high-tech supply chains lag, and the Gulf and Middle East face sharp contractions.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Favor AI-supply-chain and non-Gulf energy exporters; importers and low-income countries are vulnerable.
insights.locator: Energy and AI are driving the winners and losers; The IMF hands developing economies a tough task

insights.claim: The IMF's downside scenarios show a full oil-shipment recovery delayed to end-2027 with rising long yields cutting global growth by 0.5 point and adding 1 point to inflation, while a downward revision of AI productivity gains would cut global activity by over one point, concentrated in the US and Asia.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The AI-correction scenario is the larger macro tail risk than the energy scenario.
insights.locator: Optimistic growth projections send the wrong message

insights.claim: Central banks face supply-driven inflation from deficits, tariffs, conflicts and climate shocks that rate hikes cannot fix, so price stability needs coordination across monetary, fiscal, trade and industrial policy.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Policy mix conflicts could force central banks to sacrifice investment and growth.
insights.locator: The new geoeconomics of inflation

themes.theme: Rates, bonds and equity valuation risk

insights.claim: Three concurrent shocks, energy supply, AI demand for capital and public debt, are pushing up long-term rates: US 10-year yields hit 5.31 percent on October 5, the highest since 2002, with equilibrium real rate r* near 2.95 percent and inflation premium near 2.36 percent.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Higher-for-longer long rates threaten rich equity valuations.
insights.locator: Three shocks are pushing up long-term interest rates

insights.claim: Global AI investment spending is estimated by Goldman Sachs to exceed $1 trillion in 2026 (0.9 percent of global GDP), rising to 1.3 percent in 2027 and 1.4 percent in 2028.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: AI capex is a major driver of GDP and of borrowing demand.
insights.locator: Three shocks are pushing up long-term interest rates

insights.claim: US equities are richly valued with S&P 500 P/E around 26.6 versus a 16.2 average and Shiller CAPE above 41, with ten top companies approaching 40 percent of the index and AI/high-tech capex (1.8-2.5 percent of GDP) contributing about half of recent US GDP growth.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Concentration plus high rates makes a correction systemic.
insights.locator: Three shocks are pushing up long-term interest rates

insights.claim: Government 10-year yields have risen about 1.5 points in France, 1.25 points in the US and 0.65 points for emerging economies ex-China, and bond yields are at two-decade highs across the board.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Rising sovereign borrowing costs pressure fiscal trajectories, particularly in France.
insights.locator: The global economic safety cushions are wearing thin; The sun is no longer shining

insights.claim: Debt burdens are at post-WWII-like levels: G7 public debt is 124 percent of GDP, advanced-economy sovereign debt nearly 110 percent (US 126 percent), and global debt near 100 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Little fiscal room means spending cuts or higher taxes as rates stay high.
insights.locator: Energy and AI are driving the winners and losers; How advanced economies' surging debt is impacting emerging markets

insights.claim: The IMF Global Financial Stability Report finds AI-related technology firms hold 10 percent of global investment-grade corporate bonds (versus 1 percent in 2024), and hedge funds held about 9 percent of US government bonds in 2025, more than double 2022.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Bond-market concentration in AI debt and leveraged holders is a stress channel.
insights.locator: The global economic safety cushions are wearing thin

insights.claim: An IMF stress test combining an AI crash, an energy shock and higher rates found 22 percent of global banking assets below the 7 percent capital line, up from 18 percent last year, with weakness in banks lending heavily to private credit and private equity.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Bank exposure to non-bank lenders is the weak link to monitor.
insights.locator: The global economic safety cushions are wearing thin

insights.claim: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said AI 'is going to fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy', pointing toward real-time nowcasting using high-frequency data such as the BIS Project Spectrum on the ECB's daily price dataset.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Central bank data practices may speed policy reaction functions.
insights.quote: fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy
insights.locator: How AI can take central banks from forecasting to nowcasting

insights.claim: Warsh gave no hint of the Fed's next rate move and said domestic price stability is his top goal, while Global South civil society argues the policy trilemma has become a dilemma where capital controls are needed to keep monetary autonomy.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Fed decisions transmit to emerging markets via global financial cycles.
insights.locator: The Global South confronts a new dilemma

insights.claim: Advanced-economy borrowing hits emerging markets through higher benchmark yields, capital outflows, currency depreciation and heavier debt service, and developing countries paid a record $415 billion in external debt interest in 2024 with $741 billion more service than new financing in 2022-24.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: EM currencies and credit are exposed to Treasury yield moves.
insights.locator: How advanced economies' surging debt is impacting emerging markets

insights.claim: Low-income countries' debt service costs surged from 6 percent to 14 percent of revenue in a decade despite lower overall debt, per IMF Managing Director Georgieva.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Distress and restructuring candidates may rise.
insights.locator: Bangkok has been relatively quiet on this far-reaching reform

insights.claim: Trump's diesel deal has Russia promising to sell the US 300,000 tonnes of diesel now, 500,000 in November and 1 million in December, but US law bans Russian energy imports, Russian refineries are damaged by Ukrainian strikes, and the extra $4.7 billion of export income is a drop in the ocean against a $62 billion fiscal deficit.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Impact on global diesel prices is minimal; signals sanctions permissiveness worth more to Moscow.
insights.locator: Russia rides into Bangkok with a valuable US diesel deal

insights.claim: Russian diesel and gasoil exports hit a ten-year low just under 600,000 tonnes in September, with one of six main refineries out of service and two at 25 percent capacity.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Russian refining capacity is the binding constraint on export growth.
insights.locator: Russia rides into Bangkok with a valuable US diesel deal

insights.claim: Oil above $100 a barrel from the Middle East conflict is lifting median one-year inflation expectations to 3.9 percent, the highest since May 2023.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Oil is feeding inflation expectations and central bank tightening.
insights.locator: Three shocks are pushing up long-term interest rates

themes.theme: Geopolitics enters the IMF-World Bank agenda

insights.claim: Atlantic Council's Josh Lipsky argues finance ministers have finally accepted that finance and geopolitics cannot be separated, with ministers asking tough questions about Iran and Saudi Arabia, though the meetings produced little concrete policy momentum.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Expect policy to reflect sanctions, imbalances and security considerations.
insights.locator: They finally get it. Closing thoughts on Bangkok

insights.claim: US Treasury Secretary Bessent skipped the Bangkok meetings, leaving Fed Chair Warsh and deputy Francis Brooke to lead the G20 finance meeting, whose US-led agenda targets China's trade surplus, energy prices via Hormuz transit, sovereign debt and digital asset regulation.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US agenda priorities signal macro imbalance pressure on China.
insights.locator: At a high-stakes meeting today, the G20 is searching for balance

insights.claim: Climate change has largely vanished from the IMF's World Economic Outlook after the Trump administration stopped supporting IMF climate loans and the World Bank retired its 45 percent climate lending goal.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Multilateral climate finance is shrinking, reducing a funding source for transition projects.
insights.locator: Climate change is missing in action from the IMF's outlook

insights.claim: The US Treasury warned the IMF away from lending that 'veers into development-policy lending' even as the new low-income Debt Sustainability Framework, starting late 2027, shows 1 percent of GDP in health/education spending lifts long-run output about 1.9 percent and infrastructure about 3 percent.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US politics may limit how much the IMF uses its new debt framework.
insights.locator: Bangkok has been relatively quiet on this far-reaching reform

insights.claim: South Korea and ASEAN are benefiting from the AI super-cycle and diverted US-China trade, but gains are concentrated in few firms, rely partly on US chip restrictions on China, and portfolio rebalancing out of Korean chip stocks pressured the won despite a growing current-account surplus.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Korean chip equity inflows create FX volatility risk if the AI trade turns.
insights.locator: Can Asian economies make the good times last?

insights.claim: ASEAN economies' share of domestic value added has been shrinking and productivity stalled despite heavy FDI under 'China + One' strategies, so converting FDI into local capabilities is the key to avoiding the middle-income trap.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Favor markets that capture domestic value-add rather than assembly.
insights.locator: To make the leap, Thailand needs to convert foreign investment

insights.claim: The World Bank says it has mobilized $112 billion of private capital, more than triple four years ago, yet the world faces a projected 800 million job shortage for new workforce entrants over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Private-capital mobilization is the Bank's strategy as public development funding declines.
insights.locator: The jobs are coming. Will the money follow?

insights.claim: The IMF Fiscal Monitor 'Taxing better to boost growth' estimates VAT reforms could yield welfare gains up to 0.8 percent of GDP in emerging markets, lower cost of capital could raise long-term growth up to 2.7 percent, and work incentive reforms could raise employment 1.2 percent.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Tax-design reform is the IMF's preferred route to revenue without growth penalties.
insights.locator: The case for taxing better, not taxing more
